title: Financial statement drills: the exam-speed toolkit
hook: The midterm is multiple choice and only the letter counts. Learn to see which formula a question wants, then do the arithmetic in one pass.
objectives: Trace any event through Assets = Liabilities + Equity and say what happens to equity.
Compute market cap, market-to-book, firm value, EPS and a share price from a constant P/E.
Compute liquidity ratios, receivable days and inventory days, and judge whether management improved.

blocks.md:
Assets = Liabilities + Equity always holds, so every event must change both sides equally. Ask two questions: where does the item live, and does it actually happen today?

> "Patrick likes these kind of tricky questions."

The ECON 106F midterm is Oct 28 and covers this material.

blocks.title: Delta buys a $20M machine: $8M cash, $12M new debt

frames.title: The event
frames.text: Delta Co. pays for a $20M machine with $8M of its cash and $12M of new long-term debt.

frames.title: The machine
frames.text: Something you buy is an asset. A machine is long-lived, so it is non-current.

frames.title: The financing
frames.text: Cash is a current asset, so it falls. New debt is a liability, so it rises.

frames.title: Check both sides
frames.text: Assets rose by $12M and liabilities rose by $12M. Equity is untouched.

blocks.prompt: What happens to Delta's equity in each event?
targets: No balance sheet change at all

items.label: Uses $9M of cash to repay $9M of long-term debt
A fire destroys $6M of uninsured inventory
A competitor announces a price cut that will undercut Delta
A customer owing $5M for goods already delivered goes bankrupt
Economists find a pricing policy that will lift revenue 10%
Buys a $20M machine with $8M cash and $12M new debt

blocks.why: Losses you absorb yourself hit equity. Swapping one asset or liability for another does not. Future-looking news changes nothing on the balance sheet today.

blocks.q: A fire destroys $6M of inventory, but the insurer will pay the full $6M. What happens to equity?
options: It falls by $6M, because the inventory is physically gone
It is unchanged: the claim replaces the lost inventory
It rises by $6M because the insurance payout arrives
It is unchanged, but liabilities fall by $6M instead
blocks.why: The TA's contrast: uninsured, you lose your own money and equity falls. Insured, you recover it, so equity does not fall.

blocks.md:
Market capitalization is shares outstanding times the market price. Market-to-book divides that by book value of equity. You are given the formulas, so the skill is applying them fast.

> "You don't need to memorize everything, but you need to know how to apply these equations."

frames.title: The formula
frames.text: Quark has 8 billion shares in both years. Book equity was $100B in 2020 and $120B in 2023.
Price was $15.
Price was $27. The change is the later year minus the earlier year.

frames.title: Market-to-book
frames.text: Divide market cap by book equity in each year.

blocks.title: Market cap = shares x price
blocks.caption: At 8B shares and $27 the market cap is $216B. Each $1 of price adds $8B.

blocks.headline: Largest Companies by Market Cap in 2026
blocks.tieIn: The page lists Nvidia at a $5.65 trillion market cap as of October 2, 2026, and says it counts publicly traded shares outstanding only. That is the same shares-times-price formula you just used, scaled up. The page also shows a table figure of $5.8 trillion, so treat the exact number as approximate.

blocks.q: Quark's market cap is $216B and its book equity is $120B. What is market-to-book?
blocks.why: 216 / 120 = 1.80. Flipping the fraction gives 0.56, which is the usual slip.

steps.title: Firm value: add debt, subtract cash

blocks.md:
Firm (enterprise) value = market cap + debt - cash. Market value of equity is another name for market cap.

Why net out cash? Buy a firm and you take on its debt, but you also get its cash. The TA's toy case: market cap 10, debt 4, cash 2.

> "Supposedly it doesn't matter which source of financing you have."

frames.title: Toy case from section
frames.text: Market cap 10, debt 4, cash 2. A buyer pays for the equity, inherits the debt, and gets the cash.

frames.title: Quark, 2020
frames.text: Market cap $120B, debt $90B, cash $20B.

frames.title: Quark, 2023
frames.text: Market cap $216B, debt $40B, cash $30B.

frames.title: The change
frames.text: Equity value rose $96B, but Quark paid down $50B of debt and piled up $10B more cash.

blocks.q: Why does firm value subtract cash instead of adding it?
options: Cash is a liability, so it counts against the firm's value
Cash always earns less than debt costs, so it is penalized
A buyer gets the cash back, so it lowers the net price paid
Accountants require every asset to be subtracted from equity
blocks.why: Debt is added because you inherit it. Cash is netted because you get it back, so the operating business costs you less.

blocks.md: A common chain: sales and margin give EBIT, EBIT less interest and tax gives net income, net income over shares gives EPS, and the P/E ratio turns EPS into a price. When the question says P/E is unchanged, compute it from the earlier year first.

blocks.title: Orbit Inc: 2025 sales +10%, margin falls to 10%

frames.title: Last year as baseline
frames.text: 2024: sales $80,000, EBIT margin 12%, interest $1,600, tax 25%, 2,000 shares, price $48. EBIT is $9,600.

frames.title: P/E from last year
frames.text: Price over EPS in 2024. This stays fixed in 2025.

frames.title: New sales and EBIT
frames.text: Sales grow 10%. Use the new margin directly, no need to rebuild every cost line.

frames.title: Net income and EPS
frames.text: Interest is unchanged and the tax rate is the same.

frames.title: The price
frames.text: Sales rose, yet the price falls, because margin fell faster.

blocks.title: 2025 share price vs EBIT margin (P/E fixed at 16)
blocks.caption: At 10% the price is $43.20. Holding the 12% margin would give $53.76.

blocks.q: P/E and share count are unchanged, but net income falls 10%. What happens to the share price?
options: It falls 10%, because EPS falls 10%
It rises, since fewer earnings mean a lower P/E
It is unchanged, because P/E is held constant
It falls by more than 10% since P/E is squared
blocks.why: Price = P/E x EPS. With P/E and shares fixed, EPS and price move together.

blocks.md:
Current, quick and cash ratios get stricter in that order, so each is smaller than the last. For AR days and inventory days, **lower is better**: you want to be paid soon and not sit on stock.

> "You want those numbers to be the lowest possible."

frames.title: The balance sheet
frames.text: Cash and short-term investments $20, receivables $60, inventory $70, current liabilities $100.

frames.title: Current ratio
frames.text: All current assets over current liabilities.

frames.title: Quick ratio
frames.text: Drop inventory. Keep cash and receivables.

frames.title: Cash ratio
frames.text: Only cash and short-term investments. The denominator never changes.

frames.title: AR days, year A
frames.text: Receivables $9,000, revenue $109,500.

frames.title: AR days, year B
frames.text: Receivables $14,400, revenue $120,000.

frames.title: Inventory days, both years
frames.text: Use cost of goods sold, not revenue.

frames.title: Verdict
frames.text: Both numbers rose, so management got worse. A high number is not always bad, but across two periods it is.

blocks.title: Inventory days = inventory / COGS x 365
blocks.caption: More COGS for the same stock means faster turnover and fewer days.

blocks.q: A peer has current 1.1, quick 0.6 and cash ratio 0.1. How does Orbit (1.5, 0.8, 0.2) compare?
options: Orbit is less liquid on every ratio
Orbit is more liquid on every ratio
Orbit is more liquid on only the current ratio
The ratios cannot be compared across firms
blocks.why: Orbit has more liquid assets relative to current liabilities on all three measures.

recap: Every event keeps Assets = Liabilities + Equity balanced. Future-looking news changes nothing today.
Market cap = shares x price. Firm value = market cap + debt - cash.
With P/E fixed, price = P/E x EPS. Work out last year's P/E first.
Current, quick and cash ratios shrink in that order. For AR days and inventory days, lower is better.

quiz.q: A firm has market cap $50B, debt $30B and cash $12B. What is its firm value?
A firm buys a $10M machine with $4M of cash and $6M of new debt. What is the effect on equity?
options: No change
Falls by $4M
Rises by $10M
Falls by $6M
quiz.why: Assets rise by 10 - 4 = 6 and liabilities rise by 6. Equity does not change.

quiz.q: EPS is $2.50 and the P/E ratio stays at 18. What is the share price?
Cash and short-term investments $10, receivables $30, inventory $40, current liabilities $50. What is the quick ratio?
quiz.why: (10 + 30) / 50 = 0.8. Adding inventory would give the current ratio, 1.6.

quiz.q: Inventory is $15,000 and COGS is $73,000. What are the inventory days?
options: 0.21 days
30 days
75 days
365 days

flashcards.back: Assets = Liabilities + Equity. Every event changes both sides equally. Future-looking news changes nothing.
Market cap = shares outstanding x price. Market-to-book = market cap / book value of equity.
Market cap + debt - cash. A buyer inherits the debt and gets the cash back.
EPS = net income / shares. Price = P/E x EPS. Net income = (EBIT - interest) x (1 - tax rate).
Current = current assets / CL. Quick = (cash + receivables) / CL. Cash = cash / CL. Each is stricter and smaller.
AR days = AR / revenue x 365. Inventory days = inventory / COGS x 365. Lower is better when comparing periods.
